<reason>Side A found the sharpest available reframe — that PRO's own "regulate the product, not the technique" principle argues against a technique-defined lane, so relief should be earned by evidence within one risk-neutral framework. That turn was genuinely damaging and forced B to defend the category as such. But A's route reduced to a counterplan with almost no unique offense: its only harm story (edit size ≠ consequence size; irreversibility of planted seed) was raised in the opening and then largely abandoned, and B blunted the information-gap version with escalation triggers on known gene function plus the existing cultivar system (multi-season trials, glycoalkaloid/erucic acid style limits). B, by contrast, kept live offense (delay costs, concentration of the technology in firms that can amortise nine-figure dossiers) and converted A's counterplan into its own advantage: either A's published low-risk eligibility criteria simply are streamlined rules distinct from the GMO dossier, or A's symmetry demand reopens the regulation of conventional and mutagenised breeding — which A conceded in A4.2 and never showed to be deliverable. B's "defaults are gatekeeping, not paperwork; the tenth applicant shouldn't pay for the first nine" and the Ibadan cassava breeder framing made the comparative stakes concrete in a way A's "affordable scrutiny, not presumed safety" did not. Both sides answered pressure questions directly with proper A1:/A2: labelling and honestly conceded where testing is still required, which narrowed the clash usefully. Costs against B: its Rebuttal 2 was clipped for length, and its "went unanswered" jab about mutagenesis was chronologically premature since A had no substantive turn in between. Those are real but small next to B's cleaner comparative payoff.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q2 and its follow-through: forcing A to say whether radiation/chemical-mutagenised crops must also earn lighter treatment. A answered "yes" honestly, but that answer exposed that A's technique-neutral symmetry requires reopening ordinary plant-breeding regulation, letting B close with the deliverability contrast — a cheap disclose-and-screen default available now versus an elegant symmetry contingent on rewriting seed law.</best_rebuttal>
